title: Vitamin B6 and Alcohol: Hangover Myth, Depletion, and Safe Dose
excerpt: Does vitamin B6 help with hangovers? What alcohol does to your B6, what the old pyritinol study really found, how much B6 is safe, and when too much harms nerves.
metaDescription: Does vitamin B6 help hangovers? How alcohol depletes B6, what the pyritinol study really found, safe doses, and why too much B6 can damage nerves.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** vitamin B6 and alcohol are safe to have in the same day for almost everyone. There's no dangerous chemical clash between a normal B6 supplement and a few drinks. The real relationship runs the other way: regular heavy drinking lowers your body's supply of active vitamin B6, and people who drink a lot are one of the groups most likely to run low. As for hangovers, there is no good evidence that ordinary vitamin B6 prevents or treats one. The research people cite is a single small study from the early 1970s on **pyritinol**, a lab-made relative of B6 taken at a dose far above what's in any vitamin pill. This guide explains what alcohol does to B6, what that old study actually found, how much B6 is sensible, and why taking a lot of it can backfire.

**The quick rules:** Food and a normal multivitamin cover most people's B6 needs. If you take a B6 or B-complex supplement, keep your total from all sources under **100 mg a day**, the US upper limit for adults, and much lower is fine. Don't megadose B6 before a night out hoping to dodge a hangover. If you drink heavily most days, the low-B6 problem is real, and it's worth asking a doctor about checking your vitamin levels rather than guessing.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking vitamin B6 supplements if** you take levodopa, seizure medicines such as phenytoin or phenobarbital, or the tuberculosis drug isoniazid; you are pregnant or taking a prescription morning-sickness pill that contains B6; you have kidney or liver disease; or you drink three or more drinks most days. **See a doctor promptly if** you notice numbness, tingling, burning, or a loss of balance in your hands or feet, especially while taking B6 supplements. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Alcohol and Vitamin B6 Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Vitamin B6 isn't one molecule. It's a small family of related compounds (pyridoxine, pyridoxal, and pyridoxamine). The form your body actually uses is called **pyridoxal 5'-phosphate**, usually shortened to **PLP**. PLP is a helper molecule for well over a hundred enzymes. Among other jobs, it helps you:

- Break down and build amino acids, the building blocks of protein
- Make brain chemical messengers such as serotonin, dopamine, and GABA (the main calming signal in the brain)
- Release stored sugar from the liver and muscles for energy
- Build hemoglobin, the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen
- Keep homocysteine, an amino acid linked to heart and blood vessel health, in check

Alcohol gets in the way of this system in a few ways.

### 1. Acetaldehyde speeds up B6 breakdown

When your liver processes alcohol, the first by-product is **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that's a big part of why heavy drinking feels so bad. Research going back to the 1970s, including work by Lumeng and Li published in the *Journal of Clinical Investigation*, showed that acetaldehyde pushes PLP off the proteins that normally hold onto and protect it. Once PLP is loose, it gets broken down and flushed out faster. The net effect is that heavy drinkers burn through their active B6 more quickly than non-drinkers.

### 2. Heavy drinking often means eating less

B6 is found in a wide range of foods, so true deficiency is uncommon in people who eat a varied diet. But regular heavy drinking tends to crowd out real food, because alcohol supplies calories without nutrients. Less food in means less B6 in.

### 3. Liver damage makes it harder to store and activate B6

The liver is where much of your B6 is converted into PLP and stored. When drinking damages the liver over time, as in fatty liver or alcohol-related hepatitis, it becomes less able to do that job. Low PLP is commonly reported in people with alcohol-related liver disease.

### What this means for a social drinker

The important point is scale. The B6-lowering effect is a problem of **regular heavy drinking over months or years**, not a single night out. If you have a few drinks on a Saturday and eat normally the rest of the week, your B6 stores are very unlikely to be the reason you feel rough on Sunday. National nutrition authorities, including the US National Institutes of Health's Office of Dietary Supplements, list people with alcohol dependence among the groups most likely to have low B6, alongside people with kidney problems and certain autoimmune conditions. Occasional drinkers are not on that list.

## Does Vitamin B6 Help With Hangovers? The Pyritinol Study

If you've read that B6 "cures hangovers," the claim almost always traces back to one study. It's worth knowing what that study actually did.

### What the study tested

In 1973, a team of researchers (Khan and colleagues) published a small double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in the *Quarterly Journal of Studies on Alcohol*. They gave volunteers either **pyritinol** or a placebo around a night of drinking at a party, then compared hangover symptoms the next morning. The pyritinol group reported fewer hangover symptoms.

### Why it doesn't tell you much about your vitamin

There are several reasons this result doesn't translate to a B6 pill from the drugstore:

- **Pyritinol is not vitamin B6.** It's a semi-synthetic compound made of two B6-like molecules joined together. It was developed as a drug, and in some European countries it has been sold as a prescription medicine for memory and brain function. Your body does not handle it exactly the same way it handles ordinary pyridoxine.
- **The dose was enormous.** The study used a dose reported as around 1,200 mg of pyritinol, which is many hundreds of times the daily B6 requirement and far above any normal supplement.
- **It was one small study, done once.** Small single trials often don't hold up when repeated, and this one has never been convincingly replicated with modern methods.
- **It's half a century old.** Hangover research methods, including how symptoms are measured and how drinking is standardized, have changed a lot since then.

When researchers have reviewed the hangover-remedy evidence as a whole, the picture is weak across the board. A systematic review of randomized trials published in the *BMJ* in 2005 (Pittler and colleagues) looked at pyritinol along with other remedies and concluded that no compound had convincing evidence for preventing or treating hangovers. Later reviews of hangover treatments have reached similar conclusions: some ingredients show small hints of benefit in single studies, but none has solid, repeated evidence.

### So, should you take B6 for a hangover?

There is no good evidence that standard vitamin B6 prevents or treats a hangover. It won't hurt at a normal dose, and if your diet is poor it's a sensible nutrient to cover. But a hangover is mostly driven by things B6 doesn't touch: dehydration, poor sleep, acetaldehyde, inflammation, and stomach irritation. You'll get more out of water, food, and sleep than out of a B6 tablet.

## Vitamin B6 for Nausea After Drinking

B6 does have one well-established use related to nausea: **morning sickness in pregnancy**. Major obstetric groups, including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, include pyridoxine as a first-line option for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, and a prescription combination of pyridoxine with the antihistamine doxylamine is approved for that use.

That has led some people to try B6 for the queasy stomach after drinking. The honest answer is that hangover nausea has a different cause. It comes mainly from alcohol irritating the stomach lining, acetaldehyde, and low blood sugar. There's no good research showing B6 helps with it. Two important cautions:

- **Don't drink while pregnant.** If you're taking B6 for morning sickness, alcohol isn't part of the picture at all. No amount of alcohol has been shown to be safe during pregnancy.
- **Don't mix the prescription combo with alcohol.** The doxylamine in that morning-sickness pill is a sedating antihistamine, the same type found in many sleep aids. Alcohol is also a sedative, and stacking the two can make you much drowsier than expected.

For practical relief, our [guide to hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what actually helps settle your stomach.

## Can Vitamin B6 Help With Alcohol-Related Anxiety or Mood?

B6 is needed to make serotonin and GABA, two brain chemicals tied to mood and calm. Alcohol also acts on the GABA system, which is part of why "hangxiety," the anxious, on-edge feeling the day after drinking, is so common. It's tempting to connect those dots and assume B6 will smooth out the anxiety.

There's no good evidence that it does. Making enough serotonin and GABA depends on having *adequate* B6, not extra. If your B6 levels are already normal, adding more doesn't push brain chemistry further in your favor. The anxiety after drinking is mainly a rebound effect: alcohol dampens your brain's excitable signals while you drink, and they bounce back harder as it wears off. Sleep, time, and drinking less are what reliably help. If you have persistent anxiety or low mood, that's worth raising with a doctor whether or not you drink.

## Vitamin B6 and Liver Health

B6 has a supporting role in liver metabolism, and low B6 is common in people with alcohol-related liver disease. But there's no good evidence that taking B6 supplements protects your liver from alcohol. Correcting a real deficiency is good medicine. Taking extra when you're not deficient isn't a liver treatment.

In people with serious alcohol-related liver disease, doctors usually look at the whole nutritional picture, including B6, thiamine (B1), folate, B12, and zinc, rather than one vitamin. That's done with blood tests and medical supervision, not guesswork. If you drink heavily and are worried about your liver, our guide to [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking) explains the symptoms that deserve a doctor's attention.

## How Much Vitamin B6 Do You Need?

These are general figures from the US National Institutes of Health's Office of Dietary Supplements. They're not personal advice.

| Group | Recommended daily amount | Upper limit (all sources) |
|---|---|---|
| Adults 19 to 50 | 1.3 mg | 100 mg |
| Men 51 and older | 1.7 mg | 100 mg |
| Women 51 and older | 1.5 mg | 100 mg |
| Pregnant | 1.9 mg | 100 mg |
| Breastfeeding | 2.0 mg | 100 mg |

A few things jump out:

- **Your daily need is tiny.** About 1.3 to 1.7 mg covers most adults. Many B-complex and "energy" supplements contain 25, 50, or even 100 mg per serving, which is dozens of times what you need.
- **Food gets most people there.** Good sources include chicken, turkey, tuna, salmon, chickpeas, potatoes, bananas, fortified breakfast cereals, and beef liver. A day with a couple of these foods often meets the target without any pill.
- **The upper limit covers everything combined.** Add up your multivitamin, B-complex, energy drinks, and any "hangover" or "recovery" product, because B6 shows up in all of them.

## The Risk Most People Miss: Too Much Vitamin B6

B6 is water-soluble, so people often assume the extra just washes out harmlessly. That isn't entirely true. Taking high doses of B6 for a long time can damage nerves, a condition called **peripheral neuropathy**. A widely cited 1983 report in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Schaumburg and colleagues) described people who developed serious sensory nerve damage after taking very high doses of pyridoxine for months. The US upper limit of 100 mg a day is set to stay well clear of this.

Since then, cases have also been reported at lower doses taken over long periods, and some countries have grown more cautious. Australia's medicines regulator, for example, has issued safety warnings about nerve problems linked to B6 in supplements, noting that many people didn't realize how many of their products contained it.

**Signs of too much B6 include:**

- Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
- A burning or "pins and needles" feeling
- Clumsiness, trouble with balance, or feeling unsteady when walking in the dark
- Increased sensitivity to touch, or reduced ability to feel temperature or vibration

These usually improve after stopping the supplement, though recovery can take months.

### Why this matters for drinkers

Here's the overlap that's easy to miss. Long-term heavy drinking can **also** cause peripheral neuropathy, through alcohol's direct effect on nerves and through low thiamine and other B vitamins. That means someone who drinks heavily and takes high-dose B6 "to protect their nerves" could make tingling worse rather than better, and it can be hard to tell which is the cause. If you have numb, tingling, or burning feet or hands, don't self-treat with more vitamins. See a doctor. Our article on [tingling after drinking](/never-hungover/tingling-after-drinking) explains the short-term and long-term causes.

## Medication Interactions to Know About

Vitamin B6 interacts with a handful of medicines, and some of these are commonly taken by people who drink:

- **Levodopa (for Parkinson's disease).** Taken on its own, pyridoxine can reduce how well levodopa works. Most people now take levodopa combined with carbidopa, which largely prevents this, but check with your doctor or pharmacist.
- **Phenytoin and phenobarbital (seizure medicines).** High doses of B6 can lower the blood levels of these drugs. Alcohol can also affect seizure control, so this combination deserves a doctor's input.
- **Isoniazid (for tuberculosis).** This drug can lower B6 levels, and doctors often prescribe B6 alongside it. Isoniazid also carries liver risks that alcohol can add to, so follow your prescriber's advice on drinking closely.
- **Theophylline (for some lung conditions).** It can lower B6 levels.
- **The prescription morning-sickness pill** (pyridoxine plus doxylamine). The sedating ingredient adds to alcohol's drowsiness, as described above.

If you take any of these, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before adding a B6 supplement, and ask specifically about alcohol. For broader context on supplements and medication safety, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Who Might Actually Benefit From More B6?

Most social drinkers who eat a normal diet don't need extra B6. The people more likely to run low, and who should ask a doctor about testing rather than guessing, include those who:

- Drink **three or more drinks most days**, or binge drink regularly
- Have **alcohol-related liver disease** or have been told their liver enzymes are high
- Have **kidney disease**, especially if on dialysis
- Have **autoimmune conditions** such as rheumatoid arthritis
- Eat a very **limited diet**, or skip meals often

**Signs of low B6** can include cracks at the corners of the mouth, a sore or swollen tongue, a scaly skin rash, low mood, confusion, tiredness, and a type of anemia. These symptoms overlap with many other conditions, including other vitamin deficiencies common in heavy drinkers, which is another reason to get a blood test rather than self-diagnose. Low B6 rarely happens on its own; it often comes along with low B12, folate, and thiamine. Our guides to [thiamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/thiamine-and-alcohol) and [vitamin B12 and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol) cover the other B vitamins drinking affects most.

## B6 in Hangover Supplements: What to Look For

Many hangover and "recovery" products include B6, usually as part of a B-complex blend alongside other vitamins and plant extracts. That's not a bad thing on its own, but a few habits help:

1. **Read the milligrams.** Check how much B6 is in one serving and multiply by how many servings you'd take. Some products contain several times the daily requirement per serving.
2. **Add up your stack.** If you also take a multivitamin, a B-complex, or drink energy drinks, add those together. Stay well under 100 mg a day total.
3. **Don't credit the B6 for the effect.** If a product helps you, it isn't likely to be because of the B6. The evidence for B6 itself in hangovers is thin.
4. **Watch for "megadose" marketing.** Products that brag about delivering thousands of percent of your daily value of B vitamins aren't giving you more benefit, and in the case of B6 can add risk over time.

If you'd rather cover your bases simply, a standard multivitamin with food usually provides enough B6. Our guide to [multivitamins and alcohol](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol) and our broader look at [vitamins for hangovers](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) explain which nutrients matter most for drinkers.

## When to See a Doctor

> **See a doctor if:** you have numbness, tingling, burning, or poor balance in your hands or feet, whether or not you take B6; you take B6 supplements over 50 mg a day for more than a few weeks; you drink three or more drinks most days and haven't had your vitamin levels or liver checked; you notice signs of deficiency such as a sore tongue, cracked mouth corners, or unexplained low mood and tiredness; or you take levodopa, seizure medicines, or isoniazid and want to add a supplement. **Get emergency help (call 911) if** someone who has been drinking has a seizure, becomes very confused, can't stay awake, or has trouble breathing. Those are signs of a medical emergency, not a vitamin problem. If you've been drinking heavily every day and you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous; a doctor can help you stop safely.

## Practical Tips for Drinkers

- **Eat real food before and while you drink.** It slows alcohol absorption and gives you B6 and other nutrients at the same time. Chicken, fish, potatoes, chickpeas, and bananas are all good options.
- **Don't rely on a pill to undo a night out.** No vitamin cancels out the effects of heavy drinking.
- **Keep supplements modest.** If you take B6, the amount in a multivitamin or a low-dose B-complex is plenty for most people.
- **Pace and hydrate.** Alternate drinks with water and slow down. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.
- **If you drink most days, get a check-up.** A simple blood test can show whether you're actually low in B6 or other B vitamins.

## Where DHM Fits In

Vitamin B6 is a nutrient, not a hangover treatment. If you're looking for something to take around drinking, some people try **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. The honest picture: most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone. It doesn't replace food, water, sleep, or drinking less.

If you want to try it, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular pick, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a budget-friendly single-ingredient option. If you're also taking a B-complex or multivitamin, check each label so your total B6 stays low. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Vitamin B6 and alcohol don't have a dangerous interaction. A normal B6 supplement and a few drinks are fine together for most people.
- Regular heavy drinking lowers active B6, mainly because acetaldehyde speeds up its breakdown, heavy drinkers tend to eat less, and a damaged liver stores and activates B6 less well.
- There is no good evidence that vitamin B6 prevents or treats hangovers. The study often cited used a high dose of pyritinol, a different, drug-like compound, in one small trial from 1973.
- Adults need only about 1.3 to 1.7 mg a day. Keep your total from all sources under 100 mg a day, because long-term high doses can damage nerves.
- If you drink heavily most days, or have numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, see a doctor instead of adding more vitamins.

For how vitamin B6 fits with other supplements people take around drinking, see our guides to [milk thistle](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol), [NAC](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol), and [magnesium](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol), plus our overview of [the vitamins and minerals alcohol depletes](/never-hungover/vitamins-depleted-by-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to take vitamin B6 with alcohol?**

Yes, for most people. There's no known dangerous interaction between a normal B6 supplement and moderate drinking. Keep your total B6 from all supplements under 100 mg a day, and talk to your doctor first if you take levodopa, seizure medicines, or isoniazid, or if you drink heavily most days.

**Does vitamin B6 prevent hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that ordinary vitamin B6 prevents or treats hangovers. The claim comes from a small 1973 study that used a high dose of pyritinol, a semi-synthetic compound related to B6, not the vitamin itself. That result has not been convincingly repeated, and later reviews of hangover remedies found no compound with strong evidence.

**What is pyritinol, and is it the same as vitamin B6?**

Pyritinol is a semi-synthetic compound made of two B6-like molecules linked together. It was developed as a drug and has been sold as a prescription medicine for brain function in some European countries. It is not the same as the pyridoxine in vitamin supplements, and the dose used in the hangover study was far higher than any normal vitamin. It isn't something to self-prescribe for hangovers.

**Does alcohol deplete vitamin B6?**

Regular heavy drinking does. Acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol, speeds up the breakdown of active B6. Heavy drinkers also tend to eat less, and liver damage reduces the body's ability to store and activate the vitamin. Occasional or moderate drinkers who eat a normal diet are unlikely to become deficient.

**How much vitamin B6 is too much?**

The US upper limit for adults is 100 mg a day from all supplements combined. Taking high doses over months can cause nerve damage, with numbness, tingling, or burning in the hands and feet and problems with balance. Many supplements contain far more than the daily need of about 1.3 to 1.7 mg, so check every label and add them up.

**Can vitamin B6 help with nausea after drinking?**

There's no good evidence that it does. B6 is an established option for morning sickness in pregnancy, but hangover nausea comes mainly from stomach irritation, acetaldehyde, and low blood sugar. Water, bland food, and rest are more useful. Never combine alcohol with the prescription morning-sickness pill that pairs B6 with doxylamine, because the two add to each other's drowsiness.

**Should I take a B-complex before or after drinking?**

It doesn't matter much for a hangover, because there's no good evidence that B vitamins prevent one. If you take a B-complex for general nutrition, take it with a meal on any day. If you drink heavily on a regular basis, ask a doctor about testing for low B vitamins, especially thiamine, rather than guessing at doses.
